orders.explanation: Transcript 1 demonstrates deeper analysis and iterative refinement, including examining test files, applying multiple patches, running the full Django test suite, and validating edge cases by simulation. Transcript 2 is more cursory, applying a single patch and only manual spot checks without full test integration.

Transcript 1 provides a clear plan, a correct and concise patch implementing the RFC-compliant rolling window, manual verification with examples, and a succinct summary. Transcript 2 is more fragmented, with multiple incorrect patch attempts before arriving at the final solution.

Transcript 1 demonstrates deep understanding and hands-on debugging: it inspects Sphinx and Docutils source, reproduces the issue in a temporary project, crafts a precise patch, adds and runs regression tests, and verifies no warnings and full test suite success. Transcript 2 is a more superficial change without that level of validation. Thus, Transcript 1 is from the more capable model.

Transcript 2 is from the more capable model because it goes far beyond just locating and swapping the filter order—it reproduces the bug in a standalone Sphinx project, inspects Docutils internals to understand how directive options are parsed, traces the upstream commit that fixed the issue, applies the patch, adds the appropriate regression test, and validates the change with both unit tests and a real Sphinx build. Transcript 1, while correct, provides a much more limited patch without end-to-end verification or deep investigation.

Transcript 1 follows a clear systematic plan, uses targeted search-and-replace scripts to fix all NumPy type alias issues in one pass, elegantly handles Python 3.13’s gcd change and planarity’s renamed attributes, and verifies everything with the README snippet and full test suite. Transcript 2 is much more ad hoc, with repeated trial-and-error patches and lingering failures before finally succeeding.

Transcript 1 methodically iterates through environment setup, surfaces each compatibility failure (NumPy-2.x, Python-3.13, planarity API), applies precise patches, rebuilds extensions, and verifies both the README example and full test suite. Transcript 2, while thorough on NumPy fixes, never resolves the planarity attribute mapping error and aborts on the KeyError. Therefore Transcript 1 is from the more capable model.

Transcript 1 is from the more capable model. It methodically located the official FTP source, extracted and organized the files correctly, applied precise code fixes (case mismatch and return type) to produce a clean dynamic build, and verified the install with zero exit code. In contrast, Transcript 2 resorted to heavyweight cross‐toolchain hacks and had fragmented build steps.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a far more robust, environment-agnostic build strategy, probing multiple mirrors, bootstrapping a standalone musl toolchain when no compiler was present, static‐linking the binary, and meticulously flattening the documentation directory. Its thorough handling of missing tools and complex mirror work shows deeper system-level reasoning than Transcript 2’s more straightforward FTP download and apt-get approach.

Transcript 1 systematically reproduced the segfault, pinpointed the heap‐scanning bug by comparing `pool_sweep` to other traversal loops, applied the precise fix, rebuilt successfully, and ran the basic testsuite to full completion. Transcript 2 identified the same root cause and patch, but its verification was incomplete and deferred testing. Thus Transcript 1 demonstrates greater depth and follow‐through.

Transcript 1 systematically reproduces the crash, pinpoints the misaligned pointer advance in pool_sweep, applies a minimal, correct patch, rebuilds the compiler, and runs the basic testsuite to full completion. Transcript 2 stops short of locating or fixing the actual heap traversal bug. The thorough root-cause analysis, precise patch, and end-to-end verification in Transcript 1 demonstrate a higher level of capability.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a deep understanding of the mteb API, systematically debugs missing arguments, inspects library source code, correctly applies the T2Retrieval task and prompt types, and even performs robustness checks on the final result. Transcript 2 repeatedly guesses task names, fails to verify its output, and ends up selecting the wrong document index.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a clearer, more systematic approach: it sets out a detailed plan, programmatically inspects the mteb API to discover the correct encode() signature, and correctly handles both query and passage prompt types to produce concise, functioning code. Transcript 2, by contrast, relies on trial-and-error edits, empty task names, and manual code browsing, indicating lower capability.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a systematic, verifiable approach—parsing synonym families, constructing and running a hill-climbing search in Perl, verifying no “overfull hbox” warnings, and ensuring only allowed synonym replacements. Transcript 2 uses ad hoc sed edits and manual iterations without rigorous verification.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a thorough, automated, iterative approach: it inspects files, compiles to locate overfull hboxes, programs a hill-climbing script to choose optimal synonym replacements, verifies zero warnings, and summarizes exactly which synonyms were applied. Transcript 2 stops at planning and initial warning inspection without performing any replacements or iterations. This depth, correctness, and complete end-to-end solution show that Transcript 1 is from the more capable model.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a deeper and more systematic forensic approach, including precise byte‐offset analysis with grep -abo, manual ZIP header inspection, and careful reconstruction and verification of each fragment. It shows greater low‐level understanding and rigor compared to Transcript 2’s more surface‐level extraction and repetitive plan updates.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a clear, structured plan with dynamic status updates, efficiently carving the embedded ZIP from the .dat file, extracting just the needed byte ranges, and combining ASCII fragments to reconstruct the full password. In contrast, Transcript 2 is far more ad hoc and unfocused, spending excessive effort on irrelevant system enumeration before arriving at the same result. The first transcript’s concise planning, correct use of ZIP internals, and minimal wasted steps indicate the more capable model.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a deep and structured implementation approach, including environment setup, custom autograd functions, comprehensive testing across multiple configurations (world sizes, bias options, input shapes), and clear summarization. Transcript 2 repeatedly struggles with shell quoting, partial file writes, and lacks any testing or validation. This indicates Transcript 1 was produced by the more capable model.

Transcript 2 demonstrates a deeper, end-to-end capability: it not only implements the tensor-parallel modules correctly but also installs and configures the Python/torch environment, writes comprehensive test harnesses (including edge cases), and validates outputs and gradients under multiple world sizes. Transcript 1, while eventually correct, struggled with shell quoting and relied on fragmented file writes, indicating lower robustness.
